```diagram
{"n":"L:Load class:0:0|I:init():1:0|S:service():2:0|D:!destroy():3:0","e":"L>I:create 1 instance|I>S:ready|S>S:every request|S>D:shutdown"}
```

1. **Load** – the container loads the class and builds one instance.
2. **init()** – runs once. Open shared resources here.
3. **service()** – runs on a thread for every request and routes to doGet or doPost. Keep fields free of per-user data.
4. **destroy()** – runs once at shutdown. Release resources.

sections.title: Context, Filters, Listeners, Sessions
sections.md:
Filters run before and after servlets (auth, logging). Listeners react to events. A session is server-side memory tied to a browser by the JSESSIONID cookie.

> **Imagine:** A filter is airport security. A session is the wristband that tells staff you already checked in.

sections.title: JSP, JSTL & Legacy Views
sections.md:
JSP is HTML with Java inside that compiles to a servlet. JSTL tags replace messy scriptlets. It is legacy but still met in old systems.

> **Imagine:** A letter template with blanks. The server fills the blanks, then posts it.

sections.title: JDBC: Driver to Connection
sections.md:
JDBC is the standard way Java talks to databases. A connection is expensive, so use a DataSource with a connection pool.

> **Imagine:** Phoning a bank takes time to dial and verify you. A pool keeps a few lines open and lends them out.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Connection Pool Lifecycle (HikariCP)

```diagram
{"n":"P:Pool (idle):0:0|B:Borrowed:1:0|U:Running SQL:2:0|R:close() called:2:1|V:Reset connection:1:1|E:!Evicted, replaced:0:2","e":"P>B:getConnection()|B>U:use|U>R:finished|R>V:rollback if open|V>P:idle again|P>E:maxLifetime reached"}
```

1. **Pool** – holds idle, already-open connections. If none is free, callers wait up to connectionTimeout and then get an exception.
2. **Borrowed** – your code owns the connection, so keep this period short.
3. **Running SQL** – statements and the transaction happen here.
4. **close()** – does not close the socket. It hands the connection back.
5. **Reset** – uncommitted work is rolled back and settings are restored.
6. **Evicted** – past maxLifetime or idle timeout, the connection is closed and a fresh one is made. A leak is a borrow that never returns.

sections.title: JDBC: Statements & Transactions
Relational Theory & Modeling
sections.md:
Data lives in tables linked by keys. Normalization removes duplication so each fact is stored once.

> **Imagine:** Don’t write the customer’s address on every order slip. Store it once and let orders point to it.

sections.title: SQL DDL & Schema Objects
sections.md: CREATE and ALTER define tables, types and constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK). The database itself enforces your rules.

sections.title: SELECT Mastery
sections.md:
Joins combine tables, subqueries and CTEs break big queries into steps, and window functions calculate across rows without collapsing them.

> **Imagine:** A bank statement’s running balance: every transaction row stays visible, yet each shows the total so far. That is a window function.

sections.title: Indexing
sections.md:
An index is a separate sorted structure that makes lookups fast. B-tree is the default; GIN, GiST and BRIN suit text, geometry and huge ordered data.

> **Imagine:** A book’s index at the back: jump to the page instead of reading every page. But each new page means updating the index too.

#### Detailed explanation

Without an index PostgreSQL scans the whole table (Seq Scan). A matching index lets it jump straight to the rows. Indexes speed reads but slow writes and use disk, so add them for real query patterns only.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust ON orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
-- Index Scan using idx_orders_cust  (instead of Seq Scan)
CREATE INDEX idx_open ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'OPEN'; -- partial index
```

| Index | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| **B-tree** | equality, ranges, sorting (default) |
| **GIN** | arrays, JSONB, full-text search |
| **GiST** | geometry, ranges, nearest-neighbour |
| **BRIN** | huge tables stored in natural order, such as logs |

sections.title: Transactions, MVCC & Isolation
sections.md:
ACID keeps data correct. MVCC keeps several versions of a row so readers never block writers. Isolation levels choose how much concurrency anomaly you accept.

> **Imagine:** Like Google Docs history: you read a snapshot while someone else writes a new version.

#### Lifecycle diagram: MVCC Row Lifecycle (PostgreSQL)

```diagram
{"n":"I:INSERT, xmin set:0:0|L:Live version:1:0|U:UPDATE:2:0|NV:New version:2:1|OV:Old version, xmax set:1:1|DD:Dead tuple:1:2|VC:!VACUUM frees space:0:2","e":"I>L:commit|L>U:other tx|U>NV:writes new copy|U>OV:stamps old copy|OV>DD:no snapshot needs it|DD>VC:autovacuum"}
```

1. **Insert** – the row records the transaction that created it (xmin).
2. **Live** – visible to snapshots taken after that commit.
3. **Update** – a new row version is written.
4. **Old version** – gets an xmax and stays visible to older snapshots.
5. **Dead** – once no running transaction can see it, it is garbage.
6. **VACUUM** – marks the space reusable. Without it tables bloat.

#### Detailed explanation

Isolation levels decide which anomalies you may see. In PostgreSQL, readers use a snapshot, so they never block writers.

| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Read Committed (default)** | No | Possible | Possible |
| **Repeatable Read** | No | No | No (in PostgreSQL) |
| **Serializable** | No | No | No, may abort and need a retry |

```sql
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT balance FROM account WHERE id = 1; -- sees one stable snapshot
COMMIT;
```

sections.title: Query Planning & EXPLAIN
sections.md:
The planner picks the cheapest way to run a query. EXPLAIN shows the plan, EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows what actually happened.

> **Imagine:** A GPS choosing a route. EXPLAIN is the planned route; ANALYZE is the real trip with times.

sections.title: Functions, Procedures & Triggers
sections.md: PL/pgSQL lets you put logic inside the database. Triggers run automatically on insert, update or delete.

sections.title: Views & Materialized Views
sections.md:
A view is a saved query. A materialized view stores the result for speed and must be refreshed.

> **Imagine:** A view is a live window. A materialized view is a photograph: quick to look at, but it ages.

sections.title: PostgreSQL Internals & VACUUM
sections.md:
Updates leave old row versions behind. VACUUM cleans these dead rows so tables do not bloat.

> **Imagine:** Old drafts pile up in a bin. VACUUM is the cleaner who empties it.

sections.title: Performance Tuning
sections.md: Tune memory settings, keep statistics fresh, and watch slow queries with pg_stat_statements before changing anything.

sections.title: Replication, HA & DR
sections.md:
A primary sends changes to replicas for reads and failover. Backups plus WAL give point-in-time recovery.

> **Imagine:** A twin notebook that copies every line you write. If yours burns, the twin takes over.

sections.title: Security & Hardening
sections.md: Least-privilege roles, TLS, row-level security, and parameterised queries to stop injection.

sections.title: Spring Philosophy & IoC
sections.md:
Inversion of Control: the container creates and wires your objects instead of you using new everywhere.

> **Imagine:** A restaurant manager hires cooks and hands them tools. Cooks do not shop for their own knives.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Spring Bean Lifecycle

```diagram
{"n":"A:Instantiate:0:0|B:Inject deps:1:0|C:Aware callbacks:2:0|D:BPP before init:2:1|E:@PostConstruct:1:1|F:BPP after (proxy):0:1|G:!Ready to use:0:2|H:@PreDestroy:1:2|I:Destroyed:2:2","e":"A>B|B>C|C>D|D>E|E>F|F>G|G>H:context closes|H>I"}
```

1. **Instantiate** – the constructor runs.
2. **Inject** – dependencies and values are set.
3. **Aware callbacks** – the bean may receive its name or context.
4. **BeanPostProcessor** – hooks before and after init.
5. **@PostConstruct** – your start-up logic.
6. **After-init processor** – this is where AOP and @Transactional proxies are created.
7. **@PreDestroy** – cleanup on shutdown.

sections.title: Dependency Injection & Autowiring
AOP: Proxies & Pointcuts
sections.md:
Spring wraps beans in proxies to add logging, security or transactions around methods. A call from inside the same class skips the proxy.

> **Imagine:** A guard stands at the front door of the building. If you walk between rooms inside, you bypass the guard.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Transaction Lifecycle (@Transactional)

```diagram
{"n":"C:Caller:0:0|P:Proxy:1:0|M:Your method:2:0|CM:!COMMIT:3:0|RB:!ROLLBACK:3:1","e":"C>P:call|P>M:BEGIN|M>CM:returns normally|M>RB:RuntimeException"}
```

1. **Caller** – an outside bean calls the method (self-calls skip the proxy).
2. **Proxy** – gets a connection and begins the transaction.
3. **Method** – runs your logic.
4. **Commit** – on normal return.
5. **Rollback** – on RuntimeException or Error by default; use rollbackFor for checked ones.

sections.title: Spring MVC & DispatcherServlet
sections.md:
One front controller receives every request, finds the matching handler, runs interceptors, calls your controller and converts the result to a response.

> **Imagine:** The hotel front desk: every guest arrives there and is sent to the right department.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Spring MVC Request Flow

```diagram
{"n":"C:Client:0:0|F:Filters:1:0|DS:DispatcherServlet:2:0|HM:HandlerMapping:2:1|I:Interceptors:1:1|CT:Controller:0:1|MC:Message converter:0:2|R:!JSON response:1:2","e":"C>F:HTTP request|F>DS|DS>HM:find handler|HM>I:preHandle|I>CT|CT>MC:return value|MC>R:serialize"}
```

1. **Filters** – servlet-level work such as security and logging.
2. **DispatcherServlet** – the single front controller for all requests.
3. **HandlerMapping** – matches URL and verb to a controller method.
4. **Interceptors** – preHandle can block the request.
5. **Controller** – your method runs; arguments are bound and validated.
6. **Message converter** – Jackson turns the return object into JSON, sent back through the same layers.

sections.title: Transaction Management
Spring JDBC & JdbcTemplate
sections.md: JdbcTemplate removes connection and exception boilerplate while you still write plain SQL.

sections.title: Hibernate Architecture & Session
sections.md:
A Session tracks entities in a persistence context. Entity states: transient, managed, detached, removed. Hibernate spots changes (dirty checking) and writes them on flush.

> **Imagine:** A shopping cart: you add and remove things freely, and the shop only processes it at checkout (flush).

#### Lifecycle diagram: Hibernate Entity States

```diagram
{"n":"DB:Database:1:0|T:New / Transient:0:1|M:Managed:1:1|DT:Detached:2:1|RM:Removed:1:2|X:!Row deleted:2:2","e":"DB>M:find / query|T>M:persist()|M>DT:close / detach|DT>M:merge()|M>RM:remove()|RM>X:flush / commit"}
```

1. **Transient** – a plain object Hibernate knows nothing about.
2. **Managed** – inside a Session; dirty checking writes changes at flush.
3. **Detached** – the Session closed. Changes are ignored until merge().
4. **Removed** – scheduled for DELETE; the row goes at flush or commit.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Hibernate Flush & Commit Flow

```sequence
{"p":"A:Your code|S:Session|C:Persistence context|D:Database","m":"A>S:persist(order)|S>C:track entity + snapshot|A>S:order.setQty(5)|A>S:commit()|S>C:flush: dirty check|C>D:INSERT / UPDATE SQL|D>S:~rows written|S>D:COMMIT"}
```

1. persist() makes the entity Managed. With IDENTITY ids the INSERT may run at once.
2. A copy of its loaded state is kept for comparison.
3. Setters only change the object. No SQL yet.
4. commit() (or a query in AUTO flush mode) triggers a flush.
5. Dirty checking compares each entity with its snapshot.
6. Changed entities become INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements.
7. The database confirms the writes.
8. Only then is the transaction committed.

sections.title: Mapping: Entities & Relationships
sections.md: @Entity, @Id, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne and inheritance strategies map classes to tables. Keep the owning side clear.

sections.title: Fetching, N+1 & Caching
JPQL, HQL, Criteria & Native SQL
sections.md: JPQL queries entities, Criteria builds queries in code, and native SQL is the escape hatch for database-specific features.

sections.title: Locking & Versioning
Lifecycle Callbacks & Auditing
sections.md: @PrePersist, @PostLoad and listeners run on entity events. Auditing records who changed what and when; Envers keeps history.

sections.title: Boot Fundamentals & Auto-Configuration
sections.md:
Starters bring dependencies; auto-configuration creates beans based on what is on the classpath and in your config.

> **Imagine:** A furnished flat that rearranges itself depending on what you carry in. Add a database driver and it sets up a DataSource.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Spring Boot Startup

```diagram
{"n":"A:main():0:0|B:run():1:0|C:Load config:2:0|D:Create context:2:1|E:Auto-config + scan:1:1|F:Create beans:0:1|G:Start Tomcat:0:2|H:Run runners:1:2|I:!Ready:2:2","e":"A>B|B>C:profiles, yml|C>D|D>E|E>F|F>G|G>H|H>I"}
```

1. main() calls SpringApplication.run.
2. **Config** – application.yml, profiles and environment variables are loaded.
3. The ApplicationContext is created.
4. Component scan and auto-configuration register bean definitions.
5. Singleton beans are built (see Bean Lifecycle).
6. The embedded server starts on the port.
7. CommandLineRunner beans run, then the app is ready.

sections.title: Externalized Configuration
sections.md: application.yml, profiles and environment variables set values without rebuilding. @ConfigurationProperties binds them to typed classes.

sections.title: Embedded Servers & Runtime Tuning
sections.md: Tomcat runs inside your jar. Tune thread pools, timeouts and keep-alive for real traffic.

sections.title: Building Enterprise REST APIs
Jackson Serialization
sections.md: Converts objects to JSON and back. Annotations control names and formats. Beware lazy entities and cyclic references.

sections.title: Validation & Error Handling
Observability
sections.md:
Logs say what happened, metrics say how much, traces say where time went. Actuator exposes health and metrics.

> **Imagine:** A car dashboard: speed (metrics), warning light (health), trip log (traces).

sections.title: Testing Strategy
sections.md: Many fast unit tests, some slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest), few end-to-end. Testcontainers runs a real database in tests.

sections.title: Spring Security
sections.md:
Authentication is who you are; authorization is what you may do. Requests pass a filter chain. Know JWT, OAuth2, CSRF and password hashing (BCrypt).

> **Imagine:** Authentication is showing ID at the gate. Authorization is the badge that opens only some rooms.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Spring Security Filter Flow

```diagram
{"n":"R:Request:0:0|F1:Auth filter (JWT):1:0|SC:SecurityContext:2:0|AZ:Authorization:2:1|CT:!Controller:1:1|E1:!401:0:1|E3:!403:2:2","e":"R>F1|F1>SC:token valid|F1>E1:invalid|SC>AZ|AZ>CT:allowed|AZ>E3:denied"}
```

1. The filter reads the token (Authorization header).
2. Valid: the user is stored in the SecurityContext.
3. Invalid or missing: 401 Unauthorized.
4. The authorization rules check roles and paths.
5. Allowed: the controller runs. Denied: 403 Forbidden.

#### Lifecycle diagram: JWT Login & Request Flow

```sequence
{"p":"C:Client|F:Auth filter|S:Auth service|D:Database","m":"C>S:POST /login|S>D:load user|D>S:~stored BCrypt hash|S>S:hash matches?|S>C:~200 + signed JWT|C>F:GET /orders + Bearer token|F>F:check signature, expiry|F>C:~401 or continue to controller"}
```

1. **Login** – the client sends credentials once over HTTPS.
2. The user and password hash are loaded.
3. The hash is returned; the password is never stored in plain text.
4. BCrypt compares the typed password with the hash.
5. **Success** – a signed JWT with short expiry is returned.
6. Every later call carries the token in the Authorization header.
7. The filter verifies signature and expiry without touching the database.
8. Invalid gives 401; valid fills the SecurityContext and the request goes on.

#### Detailed explanation

Every request passes the SecurityFilterChain. Below, public paths are open, everything else needs a valid JWT. Disabling CSRF is acceptable only for stateless token APIs, not for cookie sessions.

```java
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
  return http
    .csrf(c -> c.disable())
    .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
      .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
      .anyRequest().authenticated())
    .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
    .build();
}
```

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **401** | not authenticated (who are you?) |
| **403** | authenticated but not allowed |

sections.title: Data Access: Repositories, Hikari, Migrations
sections.md:
Spring Data repositories generate queries from method names. HikariCP pools connections. Flyway or Liquibase version your schema.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Connection Pool Lifecycle (HikariCP)

```diagram
{"n":"P:Pool (idle):0:0|B:Borrowed:1:0|U:Running SQL:2:0|R:close() called:2:1|V:Reset connection:1:1|E:!Evicted, replaced:0:2","e":"P>B:getConnection()|B>U:use|U>R:finished|R>V:rollback if open|V>P:idle again|P>E:maxLifetime reached"}
```

1. **Pool** – holds idle, already-open connections. If none is free, callers wait up to connectionTimeout and then get an exception.
2. **Borrowed** – your code owns the connection, so keep this period short.
3. **Running SQL** – statements and the transaction happen here.
4. **close()** – does not close the socket. It hands the connection back.
5. **Reset** – uncommitted work is rolled back and settings are restored.
6. **Evicted** – past maxLifetime or idle timeout, the connection is closed and a fresh one is made. A leak is a borrow that never returns.

sections.title: Messaging & Async Processing
sections.md:
Queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ) decouple services. The outbox pattern saves the event and data in one transaction.

> **Imagine:** Drop a letter in a post box and walk away; the postal system delivers later, even if the receiver is out.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Outbox & Event Flow (Kafka)

```sequence
{"p":"A:Service|D:Database|R:Relay|K:Kafka|C:Consumer","m":"A>D:BEGIN: save order + outbox row|A>D:COMMIT (both or neither)|R>D:poll unsent rows|R>K:publish event|K>R:~ack|R>D:mark row sent|K>C:deliver event|C>C:process idempotently"}
```

1. One local transaction writes the business row and an outbox row.
2. Commit makes both visible together.
3. A relay (poller or CDC) finds unsent events.
4. It publishes them to the broker.
5. Kafka acknowledges.
6. The row is marked sent. A crash before this causes a duplicate.
7. Consumers receive events at least once.
8. So handlers must be idempotent, for example by checking an event id.

sections.title: Caching & Scheduling
sections.md: @Cacheable stores results (Redis, Caffeine) with expiry. @Scheduled runs jobs; use a lock so only one instance runs it.

sections.title: Deployment & Cloud-Native
sections.md:
Package as a container, use health probes, shut down gracefully, and set JVM memory to respect container limits.

#### Lifecycle diagram: Pod Lifecycle & Graceful Shutdown

```diagram
{"n":"P:Pending:0:0|S:Starting:1:0|RD:Ready:2:0|TR:Terminating (SIGTERM):2:1|DR:Drain requests:1:1|X:!Exit cleanly:0:1|K:!SIGKILL:0:2","e":"P>S:image pulled|S>RD:probes pass|RD>TR:deploy / scale-down|TR>DR:off Service|DR>X:work done|DR>K:grace period over"}
```

1. **Pending** – scheduled and the image is pulled.
2. **Starting** – the app boots; the startup probe waits for it.
3. **Ready** – the readiness probe passes and traffic arrives.
4. **Terminating** – SIGTERM is sent and the pod leaves the load balancer.
5. **Drain** – with server.shutdown=graceful Spring finishes active requests.
6. **Exit** – beans are destroyed (@PreDestroy) and the process ends.
7. **SIGKILL** – if the grace period runs out, the process is killed and open requests are cut.

sections.title: Production Debugging Playbook
sections.md:
Use thread dumps (jstack), heap dumps (MAT), GC logs and flame graphs to find hangs, leaks and slowness.

> **Imagine:** Like a doctor: take the pulse (CPU), an X-ray (heap dump), and a video of the heartbeat (thread dumps over time).

sections.title: A. Legacy-to-Modern Migration
sections.md: javax moved to jakarta (Boot 3); XML config moved to annotations and Boot; EJB and Struts moved to Spring; Hibernate 3 to 6; Java 8 to 21 features like records, virtual threads and text blocks.

sections.title: B. Production Incident Checklist
sections.md: For latency spikes, OOM, pool exhaustion, partial outages and data corruption: follow the order metrics → logs → thread/heap dumps → fix → blameless review.

sections.title: C. Capstone Project Milestones
sections.md: Phase 1: JDBC CRUD with pooling and indexes. Phase 2: Hibernate, N+1 fix, optimistic locking. Phase 3: Boot REST, validation, Actuator, Flyway, async with outbox.

sections.title: Servlet Lifecycle
sections.md:
The container, not you, controls when a servlet is created, used and destroyed.

> **Imagine:** One receptionist is hired once (init), serves visitors all day through many assistants (service), and is dismissed at closing (destroy).

```diagram
{"n":"L:Load class:0:0|I:init():1:0|S:service():2:0|D:!destroy():3:0","e":"L>I:create 1 instance|I>S:ready|S>S:every request|S>D:shutdown"}
```

1. **Load** – the container loads the class and builds one instance.
2. **init()** – runs once. Open shared resources here.
3. **service()** – runs on a thread for every request and routes to doGet or doPost. Keep fields free of per-user data.
4. **destroy()** – runs once at shutdown. Release resources.

sections.title: Spring MVC Request Flow
sections.md:
Every HTTP request travels the same path before your controller runs.

> **Imagine:** A hotel: the guest passes security (filters), the front desk (DispatcherServlet) looks up the right department, a clerk checks papers (interceptor), then the department serves them.

```diagram
{"n":"C:Client:0:0|F:Filters:1:0|DS:DispatcherServlet:2:0|HM:HandlerMapping:2:1|I:Interceptors:1:1|CT:Controller:0:1|MC:Message converter:0:2|R:!JSON response:1:2","e":"C>F:HTTP request|F>DS|DS>HM:find handler|HM>I:preHandle|I>CT|CT>MC:return value|MC>R:serialize"}
```

1. **Filters** – servlet-level work such as security and logging.
2. **DispatcherServlet** – the single front controller for all requests.
3. **HandlerMapping** – matches URL and verb to a controller method.
4. **Interceptors** – preHandle can block the request.
5. **Controller** – your method runs; arguments are bound and validated.
6. **Message converter** – Jackson turns the return object into JSON, sent back through the same layers.

sections.title: Hibernate Entity States
sections.md:
An entity is always in one of four states. Hibernate only tracks and saves changes in the Managed state.

> **Imagine:** A library book: new (not catalogued), on the shelf and tracked (managed), lent out untracked (detached), withdrawn (removed).

```diagram
{"n":"DB:Database:1:0|T:New / Transient:0:1|M:Managed:1:1|DT:Detached:2:1|RM:Removed:1:2|X:!Row deleted:2:2","e":"DB>M:find / query|T>M:persist()|M>DT:close / detach|DT>M:merge()|M>RM:remove()|RM>X:flush / commit"}
```

1. **Transient** – a plain object Hibernate knows nothing about.
2. **Managed** – inside a Session; dirty checking writes changes at flush.
3. **Detached** – the Session closed. Changes are ignored until merge().
4. **Removed** – scheduled for DELETE; the row goes at flush or commit.

sections.title: Spring Bean Lifecycle
sections.md:
The container builds each bean in a fixed order, giving you hooks at known points.

> **Imagine:** Building a car on an assembly line: frame, parts fitted, inspection, paint (proxy), road test, finally recycling.

```diagram
{"n":"A:Instantiate:0:0|B:Inject deps:1:0|C:Aware callbacks:2:0|D:BPP before init:2:1|E:@PostConstruct:1:1|F:BPP after (proxy):0:1|G:!Ready to use:0:2|H:@PreDestroy:1:2|I:Destroyed:2:2","e":"A>B|B>C|C>D|D>E|E>F|F>G|G>H:context closes|H>I"}
```

1. **Instantiate** – the constructor runs.
2. **Inject** – dependencies and values are set.
3. **Aware callbacks** – the bean may receive its name or context.
4. **BeanPostProcessor** – hooks before and after init.
5. **@PostConstruct** – your start-up logic.
6. **After-init processor** – this is where AOP and @Transactional proxies are created.
7. **@PreDestroy** – cleanup on shutdown.

sections.title: Transaction Lifecycle (@Transactional)
sections.md:
A proxy wraps your method: begin before it, commit or roll back after.

> **Imagine:** A cashier session: the till is opened before serving; at the end it is either confirmed or voided.

```diagram
{"n":"C:Caller:0:0|P:Proxy:1:0|M:Your method:2:0|CM:!COMMIT:3:0|RB:!ROLLBACK:3:1","e":"C>P:call|P>M:BEGIN|M>CM:returns normally|M>RB:RuntimeException"}
```

1. **Caller** – an outside bean calls the method (self-calls skip the proxy).
2. **Proxy** – gets a connection and begins the transaction.
3. **Method** – runs your logic.
4. **Commit** – on normal return.
5. **Rollback** – on RuntimeException or Error by default; use rollbackFor for checked ones.

sections.title: Thread Lifecycle
sections.md:
A Java thread moves between six states.

> **Imagine:** A worker: hired (NEW), working (RUNNABLE), queueing for a tool (BLOCKED), waiting for a call (WAITING), on a timed break (TIMED_WAITING), retired (TERMINATED).

```diagram
{"n":"N:NEW:0:1|R:RUNNABLE:1:1|BL:BLOCKED:2:0|W:WAITING:2:1|TW:TIMED_WAITING:2:2|TM:!TERMINATED:1:2","e":"N>R:start()|R>BL:needs lock|BL>R:got lock|R>W:wait() / join()|W>R:notify()|R>TW:sleep(ms)|TW>R:time up|R>TM:run() ends"}
```

1. **NEW** – created but not started.
2. **RUNNABLE** – running or ready to run.
3. **BLOCKED** – waiting for a synchronized lock held by another thread.
4. **WAITING** – waits until another thread signals it.
5. **TIMED_WAITING** – waits for a limited time.
6. **TERMINATED** – finished; it cannot be restarted.

sections.title: JVM Execution Pipeline
sections.md:
Source code becomes bytecode, then the JVM runs it and optimises hot parts.

> **Imagine:** Translating a book once into a universal language, then interpreters read it; popular chapters get a fast professional translation (JIT).

```diagram
{"n":"A:Hello.java:0:0|B:javac:1:0|C:.class bytecode:2:0|D:Class loader:2:1|E:Interpreter:1:1|F:JIT compiler:0:1|G:!Machine code:0:2","e":"A>B|B>C:compile|C>D:load, verify|D>E:run|E>F:hot method|F>G:optimise"}
```

1. javac compiles source into platform-neutral bytecode.
2. The class loader loads, verifies and initialises the class.
3. The interpreter starts running immediately.
4. Methods called often are marked hot.
5. The JIT compiles hot methods into native code, so long-running apps speed up.

sections.title: Object Lifecycle in GC
sections.md:
Most objects die young. The heap is split so cleanups are cheap.

> **Imagine:** A school: most notes are binned within the day (Eden). Notes that survive several clean-ups are filed in the archive (Old).

```diagram
{"n":"E:Eden (new):0:0|S:Survivor S0/S1:1:0|O:Old generation:2:0|R:!Reclaimed:1:1","e":"E>S:survives minor GC|S>S:age + 1|S>O:age limit|E>R:dead|O>R:major GC"}
```

1. new puts the object in Eden.
2. A minor GC copies live objects to Survivor and frees the rest.
3. Each survived GC raises the age.
4. At the age limit the object is promoted to Old.
5. A major or mixed GC cleans Old. Frequent full GCs signal a leak or undersized heap.

sections.title: Spring Boot Startup
sections.md:
main() starts a fixed sequence from configuration to a running web server.

> **Imagine:** Opening a shop: read the rules, build the shelves, stock the goods, unlock the door, then call the staff to their stations.

```diagram
{"n":"A:main():0:0|B:run():1:0|C:Load config:2:0|D:Create context:2:1|E:Auto-config + scan:1:1|F:Create beans:0:1|G:Start Tomcat:0:2|H:Run runners:1:2|I:!Ready:2:2","e":"A>B|B>C:profiles, yml|C>D|D>E|E>F|F>G|G>H|H>I"}
```

1. main() calls SpringApplication.run.
2. **Config** – application.yml, profiles and environment variables are loaded.
3. The ApplicationContext is created.
4. Component scan and auto-configuration register bean definitions.
5. Singleton beans are built (see Bean Lifecycle).
6. The embedded server starts on the port.
7. CommandLineRunner beans run, then the app is ready.

sections.title: Spring Security Filter Flow
sections.md:
Each request passes the security filter chain before reaching a controller.

> **Imagine:** A concert: ticket check (authentication), seat-zone check (authorization), then you enter.

```diagram
{"n":"R:Request:0:0|F1:Auth filter (JWT):1:0|SC:SecurityContext:2:0|AZ:Authorization:2:1|CT:!Controller:1:1|E1:!401:0:1|E3:!403:2:2","e":"R>F1|F1>SC:token valid|F1>E1:invalid|SC>AZ|AZ>CT:allowed|AZ>E3:denied"}
```

1. The filter reads the token (Authorization header).
2. Valid: the user is stored in the SecurityContext.
3. Invalid or missing: 401 Unauthorized.
4. The authorization rules check roles and paths.
5. Allowed: the controller runs. Denied: 403 Forbidden.

sections.title: Connection Pool Lifecycle (HikariCP)
sections.md:
A connection is opened once, lent out many times and replaced when old. close() on a pooled connection only returns it.

> **Imagine:** A library with a few lent-out laptops: you borrow one, use it, hand it back to be wiped and shelved. Very old laptops are retired and replaced.

```diagram
{"n":"P:Pool (idle):0:0|B:Borrowed:1:0|U:Running SQL:2:0|R:close() called:2:1|V:Reset connection:1:1|E:!Evicted, replaced:0:2","e":"P>B:getConnection()|B>U:use|U>R:finished|R>V:rollback if open|V>P:idle again|P>E:maxLifetime reached"}
```

1. **Pool** – holds idle, already-open connections. If none is free, callers wait up to connectionTimeout and then get an exception.
2. **Borrowed** – your code owns the connection, so keep this period short.
3. **Running SQL** – statements and the transaction happen here.
4. **close()** – does not close the socket. It hands the connection back.
5. **Reset** – uncommitted work is rolled back and settings are restored.
6. **Evicted** – past maxLifetime or idle timeout, the connection is closed and a fresh one is made. A leak is a borrow that never returns.

sections.title: Class Loading Lifecycle
sections.md:
A class goes through fixed phases before its code can run, and each phase can fail in its own way.

> **Imagine:** Opening a new shop: receive the goods (load), inspect them (verify), shelve them (prepare), label every shelf (resolve), then open (initialize).

```diagram
{"n":"L:Loading:0:0|V:Verification:1:0|PR:Preparation:2:0|RS:Resolution:2:1|IN:Initialization:1:1|US:In use:0:1|UN:!Unloaded:0:2","e":"L>V:bytes become a Class|V>PR:bytecode is safe|PR>RS:statics get defaults|RS>IN:names become references|IN>US:static blocks ran|US>UN:loader is collected"}
```

1. **Loading** – a class loader asks its parent first, then reads the .class bytes.
2. **Verification** – the JVM checks the bytecode is well formed and safe.
3. **Preparation** – static fields get default values (0, null).
4. **Resolution** – symbolic names turn into direct references.
5. **Initialization** – static initializers run once, thread-safely. A failure here gives ExceptionInInitializerError.
6. **Unloading** – only when the loader itself is garbage collected. A classic cause of leaks in redeployed apps.

sections.title: HashMap put() Flow
sections.md:
Each put() follows the same decision path, which explains both its speed and the hashCode/equals rules.

> **Imagine:** A hotel: hash picks the corridor, you check each locker in it, and equals decides whether it is your bag or a new one.

```diagram
{"n":"K:put(k, v):0:0|H:hash(k):1:0|B:Bucket index:2:0|EM:Bucket empty?:2:1|EQ:equals() match?:1:1|RP:!Replace value:0:1|NW:!Add new node:2:2|RZ:Resize check:1:2","e":"K>H|H>B:spread bits|B>EM:hash & (n-1)|EM>NW:empty|EM>EQ:occupied|EQ>RP:same key|EQ>NW:different key|NW>RZ:over 75%?"}
```

1. **hash** – hashCode() is mixed so high bits also matter.
2. **Index** – the bucket is chosen with hash & (length-1).
3. **Empty bucket** – the new node is placed straight in.
4. **Occupied** – every node in the bucket is compared with equals().
5. **Same key** – only the value is replaced.
6. **Different key** – the node is appended; a chain of 8 or more becomes a tree.
7. **Resize** – above 75% full the table doubles and entries are re-spread.

sections.title: MVCC Row Lifecycle (PostgreSQL)
sections.md:
An UPDATE never edits a row in place. It writes a new version and leaves the old one until VACUUM removes it.

> **Imagine:** Editing a shared document by saving new copies. Readers still open the old copy; a cleaner later bins copies nobody is reading.

```diagram
{"n":"I:INSERT, xmin set:0:0|L:Live version:1:0|U:UPDATE:2:0|NV:New version:2:1|OV:Old version, xmax set:1:1|DD:Dead tuple:1:2|VC:!VACUUM frees space:0:2","e":"I>L:commit|L>U:other tx|U>NV:writes new copy|U>OV:stamps old copy|OV>DD:no snapshot needs it|DD>VC:autovacuum"}
```

1. **Insert** – the row records the transaction that created it (xmin).
2. **Live** – visible to snapshots taken after that commit.
3. **Update** – a new row version is written.
4. **Old version** – gets an xmax and stays visible to older snapshots.
5. **Dead** – once no running transaction can see it, it is garbage.
6. **VACUUM** – marks the space reusable. Without it tables bloat.

sections.title: JWT Login & Request Flow
sections.md:
The server signs a token at login and later trusts it only if the signature and expiry check out.

> **Imagine:** A festival wristband: issued once at the gate after ID check, then staff just inspect the band.

```sequence
{"p":"C:Client|F:Auth filter|S:Auth service|D:Database","m":"C>S:POST /login|S>D:load user|D>S:~stored BCrypt hash|S>S:hash matches?|S>C:~200 + signed JWT|C>F:GET /orders + Bearer token|F>F:check signature, expiry|F>C:~401 or continue to controller"}
```

1. **Login** – the client sends credentials once over HTTPS.
2. The user and password hash are loaded.
3. The hash is returned; the password is never stored in plain text.
4. BCrypt compares the typed password with the hash.
5. **Success** – a signed JWT with short expiry is returned.
6. Every later call carries the token in the Authorization header.
7. The filter verifies signature and expiry without touching the database.
8. Invalid gives 401; valid fills the SecurityContext and the request goes on.

sections.title: Hibernate Flush & Commit Flow
sections.md:
Changes are collected in memory and sent to the database later, in one batch, at flush.

> **Imagine:** Shopping: items go in the basket as you pick them; the till only rings up at checkout.

```sequence
{"p":"A:Your code|S:Session|C:Persistence context|D:Database","m":"A>S:persist(order)|S>C:track entity + snapshot|A>S:order.setQty(5)|A>S:commit()|S>C:flush: dirty check|C>D:INSERT / UPDATE SQL|D>S:~rows written|S>D:COMMIT"}
```

1. persist() makes the entity Managed. With IDENTITY ids the INSERT may run at once.
2. A copy of its loaded state is kept for comparison.
3. Setters only change the object. No SQL yet.
4. commit() (or a query in AUTO flush mode) triggers a flush.
5. Dirty checking compares each entity with its snapshot.
6. Changed entities become INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements.
7. The database confirms the writes.
8. Only then is the transaction committed.

sections.title: Outbox & Event Flow (Kafka)
sections.md:
Save the data and the event together, then publish the event afterwards, so neither is ever lost.

> **Imagine:** Write a letter and put the copy in your outbox tray in one motion. A courier later takes trays to the post office.

```sequence
{"p":"A:Service|D:Database|R:Relay|K:Kafka|C:Consumer","m":"A>D:BEGIN: save order + outbox row|A>D:COMMIT (both or neither)|R>D:poll unsent rows|R>K:publish event|K>R:~ack|R>D:mark row sent|K>C:deliver event|C>C:process idempotently"}
```

1. One local transaction writes the business row and an outbox row.
2. Commit makes both visible together.
3. A relay (poller or CDC) finds unsent events.
4. It publishes them to the broker.
5. Kafka acknowledges.
6. The row is marked sent. A crash before this causes a duplicate.
7. Consumers receive events at least once.
8. So handlers must be idempotent, for example by checking an event id.

sections.title: Pod Lifecycle & Graceful Shutdown
sections.md:
On deploy or scale-down the platform stops sending traffic first and kills the app only after in-flight work finishes.

> **Imagine:** A shop closing: lock the entrance, serve people already inside, then switch the lights off.

```diagram
{"n":"P:Pending:0:0|S:Starting:1:0|RD:Ready:2:0|TR:Terminating (SIGTERM):2:1|DR:Drain requests:1:1|X:!Exit cleanly:0:1|K:!SIGKILL:0:2","e":"P>S:image pulled|S>RD:probes pass|RD>TR:deploy / scale-down|TR>DR:off Service|DR>X:work done|DR>K:grace period over"}
```

1. **Pending** – scheduled and the image is pulled.
2. **Starting** – the app boots; the startup probe waits for it.
3. **Ready** – the readiness probe passes and traffic arrives.
4. **Terminating** – SIGTERM is sent and the pod leaves the load balancer.
5. **Drain** – with server.shutdown=graceful Spring finishes active requests.
6. **Exit** – beans are destroyed (@PreDestroy) and the process ends.
7. **SIGKILL** – if the grace period runs out, the process is killed and open requests are cut.

questions.title: Two Sum
questions.statement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two different elements whose values add up to `target`. Exactly one valid pair exists, and you may return the indices in any order.
questions.approach: Store each value's index in a `HashMap` as you scan. For the current number, look up `target - nums[i]`; if it was seen earlier, you have the pair. One pass, constant-time lookups.

questions.title: Contains Duplicate
questions.statement: Return `true` if any value appears at least twice in the array, otherwise `false`.
questions.approach: `HashSet.add` returns `false` when the element is already present, so the first failed add is a duplicate. Sorting would give O(1) extra space at O(N log N) time.

questions.title: Valid Anagram
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Fixed size array `int[26]`)
questions.statement: Given two strings `s` and `t` of lowercase letters, return `true` if `t` is a rearrangement of the letters of `s`.
questions.approach: Count letters of `s` up and letters of `t` down in one `int[26]`. If the lengths match and every count ends at zero, they are anagrams. Constant space because the alphabet is fixed.

questions.title: Group Anagrams
questions.target: O(N · K) Time, O(N · K) Space (`HashMap<String, List<String>>`)
questions.statement: Group the strings in `strs` so that every group contains words that are anagrams of each other. Groups and the words inside them may be returned in any order.
questions.approach: Anagrams share the same letter-count signature. Build that signature (26 counts) as the map key, then append each word to its bucket. Sorting each word also works but costs O(K log K) per word.

questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements
questions.target: O(N) Time via Bucket Sort or O(N log K) via Min-Heap
questions.statement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` values that occur most often. The answer may be returned in any order, and it is guaranteed to be unique.
questions.approach: Count frequencies in a map, then bucket values by frequency (index = count, at most N). Walk the buckets from the highest frequency down until you have `k` values. That is O(N) with no sorting; a min-heap of size `k` is the O(N log K) alternative.

questions.title: Product of Array Except Self
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space (Prefix & Suffix products)
questions.statement: Return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of every element of `nums` except `nums[i]`. Do not use division and run in O(N).
questions.approach: Two passes. First fill `answer[i]` with the product of everything to the left of `i`. Then sweep right-to-left, multiplying by a running product of everything to the right. The output array is the only storage, so auxiliary space is O(1).

questions.title: Valid Sudoku
questions.statement: Decide whether a partially filled 9x9 Sudoku board is valid. Only filled cells are checked: no digit may repeat in a row, a column, or any of the nine 3x3 boxes. Empty cells are `'.'`. The board does not need to be solvable.

tests.input: The same board but the first row is "83..7...." (two 8s in column 0)

questions.approach: Walk all 81 cells once and record each digit with its row, column and box in a `HashSet` of encoded strings. A failed `add` means a repeat. The board size is fixed, so time and space are O(1).

questions.title: Encode and Decode Strings
questions.statement: Design `encode` and `decode` so a list of strings can be turned into one string and recovered exactly. The strings may contain any characters, including your delimiter.

tests.output: encoded "4#lint4#code4#love3#you", decoded back to the same list

questions.approach: Prefix every string with its length and a `#`. When decoding, read the number up to the next `#`, then take exactly that many characters. Because you always skip by length, a `#` inside the data is harmless.

questions.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(N) Space (`HashSet` boundary lookup)
questions.statement: Return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (such as 4,5,6,7) that can be formed from the values of `nums`, in any order. It must run in O(N).
questions.approach: Put every value in a `HashSet`. Only start counting from numbers that have no predecessor (`n - 1` absent); from there walk upward while `n + 1` exists. Each element is visited a constant number of times.

questions.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
questions.statement: Count the contiguous, non-empty subarrays of `nums` whose elements sum to `k`. Values can be negative, so a sliding window will not work.
questions.approach: Keep a running prefix sum and a map of how many times each prefix sum has occurred. A subarray ending here sums to `k` exactly when an earlier prefix equals `sum - k`, so add that count to the answer. Seed the map with `0 -> 1`.

questions.title: Sort Colors (75 Ball Sort)
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Dutch National Flag algorithm)
questions.statement: Sort an array containing only 0, 1 and 2 in place (red, white, blue) in one pass, without using a library sort.
questions.approach: Dutch National Flag: keep `lo` (next spot for 0), `hi` (next spot for 2) and a scanner `i`. Swap 0s to the front and 2s to the back; do not advance `i` after swapping with `hi`, because the swapped-in value is unchecked.

questions.title: Majority Element
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm)
questions.statement: Return the element that appears more than N/2 times in the array. A majority element is guaranteed to exist.
questions.approach: Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter. Matching values increment it, others decrement it, and at zero the next value becomes the candidate. A true majority outvotes everything else combined, so it survives. O(1) space.

questions.title: Valid Palindrome
questions.statement: A phrase is a palindrome if, after lowercasing it and removing every character that is not a letter or digit, it reads the same forwards and backwards. Return whether string `s` is a palindrome.

tests.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

questions.approach: Two pointers from both ends. Skip non-alphanumeric characters on each side, compare the lowercase characters, and move inward. No extra string is built, so space is O(1).

questions.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
questions.statement: `numbers` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the 1-based indices `[i, j]` (with `i < j`) of the two numbers that add up to `target`. Exactly one solution exists and you may not reuse an element. Use only constant extra space.
questions.approach: Start one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right; if too large, move the right pointer left. Sorting guarantees each move rules out a whole row of pairs.

questions.title: 3Sum
questions.target: O(N^2) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space (Sorting + Two Pointers)
questions.statement: Return all unique triplets `[a, b, c]` from `nums` such that `a + b + c == 0`. The result must not contain duplicate triplets.
questions.approach: Sort the array. Fix the first value `nums[i]`, then solve a two-sum with two pointers on the rest. Skip repeated values for `i`, `l` and `r` so no duplicate triplet is produced.

questions.title: Container With Most Water
questions.statement: `height[i]` is the height of a vertical line at position `i`. Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water, and return that maximum area.
questions.approach: Start with the widest container (both ends). The area is limited by the shorter line, so moving the taller line can never help; move the shorter one inward and keep the best area seen.

questions.title: Trapping Rain Water
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Two Pointers / Two Arrays)
questions.statement: `height` describes an elevation map where each bar has width 1. After it rains, return how many units of water are trapped between the bars.
questions.approach: Water above a bar equals the lower of the tallest bars on its left and right, minus its own height. Two pointers track the running left max and right max; always process the side with the smaller bar, since its limit is already known.

questions.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
questions.statement: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place so each value appears once, keeping the relative order. Return `k`, the number of unique values; the first `k` slots must hold them.
questions.approach: A slow pointer marks where the next unique value goes; a fast pointer scans. Whenever the scanned value differs from the last kept one, copy it to the slow position.

questions.title: Move Zeroes
questions.statement: Move every `0` in the array to the end while keeping the order of the non-zero elements. Do it in place.
questions.approach: Keep a write index for the next non-zero value. Scan the array, swapping each non-zero element into the write position. Zeros are pushed back automatically.

questions.title: BackSpace String Compare
questions.statement: Both strings are typed into editors where `#` acts as a backspace (it does nothing on empty text). Return whether the two strings end up equal.
questions.approach: Walk both strings from the end. For each, skip characters that are cancelled by a `#` (count pending backspaces), then compare the next real characters. No stacks or rebuilt strings, so O(1) space.

questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.statement: `prices[i]` is a stock price on day `i`. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximise profit, and return that profit (0 if no profit is possible).
questions.approach: Track the lowest price seen so far. For each day, the best profit selling today is `price - minSoFar`. Keep the maximum. One pass, O(1) space.

questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.statement: Return the length of the longest substring of `s` that contains no repeated character.
questions.approach: Sliding window with a table of each character's last seen index. When a character repeats inside the window, jump the window start just past its previous position. The window always holds unique characters.

questions.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
questions.statement: You may change at most `k` characters of uppercase string `s` to any other letter. Return the length of the longest substring that can be made of one repeated letter.
questions.approach: Keep a window and the count of its most frequent letter. The window is valid while `length - maxCount <= k` (the rest can be replaced). Otherwise slide the left edge. The max count never needs to shrink, because only a larger count can improve the answer.

questions.title: Permutation in String
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Fixed window size array matching)
questions.statement: Return `true` if `s2` contains a substring that is a permutation of `s1`.
questions.approach: Slide a fixed window of length `len(s1)` over `s2`, maintaining letter counts for the window and comparing with the counts of `s1`. Adding the new letter and removing the old one is O(1) per step.

questions.title: Minimum Window Substring
questions.statement: Return the smallest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t` (including duplicates). If none exists, return an empty string.
questions.approach: Expand the right edge until the window covers all of `t` (tracked with a `missing` counter and a need table). Then shrink from the left while it still covers everything, recording the best window each time.

questions.title: Sliding Window Maximum
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(K) Space (`ArrayDeque` monotonic queue)
questions.statement: A window of size `k` slides from the left of `nums` to the right, one position at a time. Return the maximum of each window position.
questions.approach: Keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order. Before adding index `i`, drop smaller values from the back (they can never be a max again) and drop the front if it left the window. The front is always the current maximum.

questions.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
questions.statement: Find the contiguous subarray of length exactly `k` with the largest average and return that average.
questions.approach: Compute the sum of the first `k` elements, then slide: add the new element, subtract the one leaving. Track the maximum sum and divide by `k` once at the end.

questions.title: Valid Parentheses
questions.statement: `s` contains only the characters `()[]{}`. Return whether every bracket is closed by the same type, in the correct order.
questions.approach: Push each opening bracket on a stack. For a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener. At the end the stack must be empty.

questions.title: Min Stack
questions.statement: Design a stack that supports `push`, `pop`, `top` and retrieving the minimum element, all in constant time.
questions.approach: Keep a second stack of running minimums. Every push also pushes `min(value, currentMin)`; every pop removes from both. The top of the min stack is always the current minimum.

questions.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
questions.statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression given in Reverse Polish Notation. Operators are `+ - * /`; division truncates toward zero. Every intermediate result fits in 32 bits.
questions.approach: Scan the tokens with a stack. Numbers are pushed; an operator pops the top two values (right operand first), applies the operation and pushes the result. The last value left is the answer.

questions.title: Generate Parentheses
questions.statement: Given `n` pairs of parentheses, generate every combination of well-formed parentheses.
questions.approach: Backtracking. You can add `(` while fewer than `n` have been used, and `)` only while it would not exceed the number of opens. Every path that reaches length `2n` is valid.

questions.title: Daily Temperatures
questions.statement: For each day, return how many days you must wait for a warmer temperature. If no warmer day follows, the answer for that day is 0.
questions.approach: Monotonic stack of indices with decreasing temperatures. When today is warmer than the temperature at the top index, that earlier day has found its answer (`today - index`); pop and repeat.

questions.title: Car Fleet
questions.target: O(N log N) Time, O(N) Space
questions.statement: Cars at the given `position`s drive toward `target` at their own `speed`. A faster car that catches a slower one must slow down and drive bumper to bumper, forming a fleet. Return the number of fleets that arrive at the target.
questions.approach: Sort cars by position, closest to the target first, and compute each car's arrival time. If a car would arrive later than the fleet ahead of it, it is a new fleet; otherwise it merges into that fleet.

questions.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
questions.statement: `heights[i]` is the height of a histogram bar of width 1. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside the histogram.
questions.approach: Keep a stack of indices with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, pop taller bars: each popped bar's rectangle extends from the new stack top to the current index. A sentinel height of 0 at the end flushes the stack.

questions.title: Binary Search
questions.statement: `nums` is sorted ascending with distinct values. Return the index of `target`, or -1 if it is absent, in O(log N).
questions.approach: Keep a low and high bound. Compare the middle element with the target and discard the half that cannot contain it. Compute `mid` as `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` to avoid overflow.

questions.title: Search a 2D Matrix
questions.statement: Each row of the matrix is sorted, and the first number of a row is greater than the last number of the previous row. Return whether `target` is in the matrix, in O(log(M·N)).
questions.approach: The matrix behaves like one sorted array of `rows * cols` elements. Binary search over the virtual index and convert with `row = mid / cols`, `col = mid % cols`.

questions.title: Koko Eating Bananas
questions.target: O(N log(max P)) Binary Search on Answer
questions.statement: Koko has `h` hours to eat all banana piles. At speed `k` bananas/hour she eats from one pile per hour (finishing a smaller pile wastes the rest of that hour). Return the minimum integer `k` that lets her finish within `h` hours.
questions.approach: Binary search on the answer `k` between 1 and the largest pile. For a candidate `k`, the hours needed are the sum of `ceil(pile / k)`. Feasibility is monotonic, so find the smallest feasible `k`.

questions.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.statement: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot (for example `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` became `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`). Return the minimum element in O(log N).
questions.approach: Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]`. If mid is larger, the minimum is to its right; otherwise it is at mid or to its left. Narrow until the bounds meet.

questions.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.statement: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot. Return the index of `target`, or -1 if it is not present, in O(log N).
questions.approach: At every step one half around `mid` is sorted. Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half; if so search it, otherwise search the other half.

questions.title: Time Based Key-Value Store
questions.target: O(log N) Get, O(1) Set (`TreeMap` or `ArrayList` binary search)
questions.statement: Design a key-value store where each key keeps multiple values with increasing timestamps. `set(key, value, timestamp)` stores a value; `get(key, timestamp)` returns the value whose timestamp is the largest one not greater than the query, or an empty string if none exists.
questions.approach: Store a `TreeMap<Integer, String>` per key and use `floorEntry(timestamp)` for the lookup, which is O(log N). With strictly increasing timestamps an `ArrayList` plus manual binary search gives O(1) set.

questions.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
questions.statement: Given two sorted arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return the median of all their elements combined. The running time must be O(log(min(M, N))).
questions.approach: Binary search a partition of the shorter array so that the left halves of both arrays together hold half the elements and every left value is at most every right value. Then the median comes from the four values around the cut.

questions.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
questions.statement: In a sorted array, return the `[first, last]` indices of `target`, or `[-1,-1]` if it does not occur. It must run in O(log N).
questions.approach: Run a binary search twice: once for the first index whose value is at least `target`, and once for the first index whose value is strictly greater. The range is `[first, firstGreater - 1]`, valid only if the first position holds the target.

questions.title: Reverse Linked List
questions.statement: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
questions.approach: Walk the list once, pointing each node's `next` at the node before it. Keep `prev`, `cur` and a saved `next`. O(1) extra space; recursion is the O(N)-stack alternative.

questions.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
questions.statement: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list made from the nodes of both, and return its head.
questions.approach: Use a dummy head and a tail pointer. Repeatedly attach the smaller front node of the two lists. When one list runs out, attach the remainder of the other.

questions.title: Reorder List
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Find middle, reverse 2nd half, merge)
questions.statement: Reorder a list `L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln` in place into `L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> ...`. You may not change node values, only the links.
questions.approach: Three steps: find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, then interleave the two halves node by node.

questions.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
questions.statement: Remove the `n`-th node from the end of a list and return the head.
questions.approach: Move a fast pointer `n` steps ahead, then advance both pointers until fast reaches the last node. The slow pointer is then right before the node to delete. A dummy head handles removing the first node.

questions.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space (Interleaving nodes)
questions.statement: Each node of a linked list has an extra `random` pointer that may point to any node in the list or to null. Return a deep copy: brand-new nodes whose `next` and `random` pointers reproduce the original structure.

tests.output: a deep copy with the same values and random links

questions.approach: Interleave: insert each copy right after its original, set `copy.random = original.random.next`, then split the two lists apart again. No hash map, so auxiliary space is O(1).

questions.title: Add Two Numbers
questions.statement: Two non-empty lists store non-negative integers with the digits in reverse order (least significant digit first). Add the numbers and return the sum in the same format.
questions.approach: Add digit by digit like grade-school addition, carrying into the next node. Keep going while either list has digits or a carry remains, treating missing digits as 0.

questions.title: Linked List Cycle
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare)
questions.statement: Return whether a linked list contains a cycle (some node's `next` leads back to an earlier node).
questions.approach: Floyd's tortoise and hare: move one pointer by 1 and another by 2. If there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually laps the slow one; otherwise it reaches null.

questions.title: Linked List Cycle II
questions.statement: If a linked list has a cycle, return the node where the cycle begins; otherwise return null. Do not modify the list.
questions.approach: Use Floyd's algorithm to detect a meeting point. Then restart one pointer from the head and move both one step at a time; they meet exactly at the cycle entrance, because the distance from head to entrance equals the distance from the meeting point to it around the loop.

questions.title: Find the Duplicate Number
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Floyd's cycle on array indices)
questions.statement: `nums` has `n + 1` integers, each between 1 and `n`, and exactly one value is repeated (possibly many times). Return the repeated value without modifying the array and using only O(1) extra space.
questions.approach: Treat `i -> nums[i]` as a linked list. A duplicate means two indices point to the same next node, so the list has a cycle and the duplicate value is the cycle entrance. Find it with Floyd's two phases.

questions.title: LRU Cache
questions.target: O(1) Get & Put (`HashMap` + Doubly Linked List)
questions.statement: Design a Least Recently Used cache with a fixed capacity. `get(key)` returns the value or -1; `put(key, value)` inserts or updates and evicts the least recently used key when the capacity is exceeded. Both must run in O(1).
questions.approach: A `HashMap` gives O(1) lookup of nodes; a doubly linked list keeps usage order (most recent at the front). Every access moves the node to the front; eviction removes the node before the tail sentinel.

questions.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
questions.statement: Merge `k` sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list and return it.
questions.approach: Keep a min-heap holding the current head of each list. Pop the smallest, append it to the result, and push that node's successor. Each of the N nodes costs O(log K).

questions.title: Invert Binary Tree
questions.statement: Invert a binary tree (swap the left and right child of every node) and return its root.
questions.approach: Recursively invert both subtrees and swap them. Every node is visited once; the call stack depth equals the tree height.

questions.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
questions.statement: Return the maximum depth of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
questions.approach: The depth of a node is 1 plus the larger depth of its two subtrees; an empty tree has depth 0.

questions.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
questions.statement: Return the diameter of a binary tree: the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path may or may not pass through the root.
questions.approach: For each node, the longest path through it is `height(left) + height(right)`. Compute heights bottom-up in one DFS and update a global best as you go.

questions.title: Balanced Binary Tree
questions.statement: Return whether a binary tree is height-balanced: for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.
questions.approach: Compute heights bottom-up and return -1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced, so each node is processed once instead of recomputing heights at every level.

questions.title: Same Tree
questions.statement: Return whether two binary trees are identical: same shape and same node values.
questions.approach: Compare roots, then recurse on both left children and both right children. Two null nodes match; a null against a non-null does not.

questions.title: Subtree of Another Tree
questions.statement: Return whether `subRoot` appears as a subtree of `root`: some node of `root` has exactly the same structure and values as `subRoot` (including all of that node's descendants).
questions.approach: For every node in `root`, check whether the tree rooted there is identical to `subRoot` using a same-tree comparison. Worst case O(N · M).

questions.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
questions.statement: In a binary search tree, return the lowest common ancestor of two given nodes: the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node counts as a descendant of itself).
questions.approach: Use the BST ordering. If both values are smaller than the current node, go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise the current node is where the paths split, so it is the LCA. Iterative, O(H).

questions.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
questions.statement: Return the level-order traversal of a binary tree: a list of lists, where each inner list holds one level's values from left to right.
questions.approach: Breadth-first search with a queue. Process exactly `queue.size()` nodes per round so each round is one level, adding children for the next round.

questions.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
questions.statement: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, from top to bottom.
questions.approach: Level-order BFS; the last node of each level is the one visible from the right. A DFS visiting the right child first and recording the first node at each depth also works.

questions.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
questions.statement: A node `X` is "good" if no node on the path from the root to `X` has a value greater than `X`. Return the number of good nodes in the tree.
questions.approach: DFS carrying the maximum value seen on the path so far. A node is good when its value is at least that maximum; then pass the updated maximum to its children.

questions.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
questions.statement: Return whether a binary tree is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger (strictly).
questions.approach: Pass down an allowed `(min, max)` range. Each node must lie strictly inside it; going left tightens the max, going right tightens the min. Checking only direct children is not enough (see the third case). Use `long` bounds so `Integer.MIN_VALUE` and `MAX_VALUE` nodes work.

questions.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
questions.statement: Return the `k`-th smallest value (1-indexed) in a binary search tree.
questions.approach: In-order traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order. Walk it iteratively with a stack and stop at the `k`-th node, which costs O(H + K).

questions.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
questions.statement: Given the preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree with unique values, rebuild and return the tree.
questions.approach: The first preorder value is the root. Its position in the inorder array splits left and right subtrees. A map from value to inorder index gives O(1) splits, and a moving preorder pointer picks each next root.

questions.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
questions.statement: A path in a binary tree is any sequence of connected nodes, going through each node at most once, and it need not pass through the root. Return the maximum sum of node values over all non-empty paths.
questions.approach: For each node compute the best downward path starting there (`node + max(0, bestLeft, bestRight)`). The best path bending at the node is `node + max(0, left) + max(0, right)`; track the global maximum. Negative branches are ignored.

questions.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
questions.statement: Design `serialize` and `deserialize` for a binary tree: convert the tree to a string and rebuild exactly the same tree from that string. You choose the format.
questions.approach: Pre-order DFS, writing `#` for null children. Because pre-order plus explicit nulls is unambiguous, deserialization consumes the tokens in the same order and rebuilds recursively.

questions.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
questions.target: O(L) Insert/Search where L is word length
questions.statement: Implement a Trie (prefix tree) with `insert(word)`, `search(word)` (exact match) and `startsWith(prefix)`. All input is lowercase letters.
questions.approach: Each node holds 26 child links and an `isWord` flag. Every operation walks one node per character, so it costs O(L) for a word of length L.

questions.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
questions.statement: Design a data structure supporting `addWord(word)` and `search(pattern)`, where the pattern may contain `.` that matches any single letter.
questions.approach: Store words in a trie. For a normal letter follow one child; for `.` try every child recursively (DFS). Worst case grows with the number of wildcards, but ordinary lookups stay O(L).

questions.title: Word Search II
questions.statement: Given a grid of letters and a list of words, return every word that can be traced in the grid through horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell at most once per word.
questions.approach: Put all words in a trie, then DFS from every cell while walking the trie. A branch with no matching trie child is abandoned immediately, which prunes most of the search. Clear a word from its node once found to avoid duplicates.

questions.title: Subsets
questions.statement: Return all subsets (the power set) of an array of distinct integers. The result must not contain duplicate subsets; any order is accepted.
questions.approach: Backtracking: at each step record the current subset, then try adding each later element, recurse, and remove it. Choosing only from indices after the last pick prevents duplicates. There are 2^N subsets.

questions.title: Combination Sum
questions.statement: Given distinct positive integers `candidates` and a `target`, return every unique combination whose numbers sum to `target`. Each number may be used any number of times.
questions.approach: Backtrack with a start index. Reusing the same number means recursing with `i` (not `i + 1`); moving the start forward avoids permutations of the same combination. Stop when the remaining amount hits 0.

questions.title: Permutations
questions.statement: Return all permutations of an array of distinct integers, in any order.
questions.approach: Build each permutation position by position, choosing any value not yet used (tracked with a boolean array), recursing, then un-choosing. N! results of length N.

questions.title: Subsets II
questions.statement: `nums` may contain duplicates. Return all possible subsets without duplicate subsets, in any order.
questions.approach: Sort first so equal values are adjacent. In the loop, skip `nums[i]` when it equals `nums[i-1]` and `i > start`: that value was already tried at this depth, so using it again would repeat a subset.

questions.title: Word Search
questions.statement: Return whether `word` can be built by walking through horizontally or vertically adjacent cells of the grid, never using the same cell twice.
questions.approach: DFS from every cell that matches the first letter. Mark the current cell as used while exploring its four neighbours, then restore it when backtracking.

questions.title: Palindrome Partitioning
questions.statement: Partition string `s` so that every piece is a palindrome, and return all possible partitionings.
questions.approach: Backtracking over cut positions: from the current start, try every end index; if `s[start..end]` is a palindrome, take it and recurse on the rest. When the start reaches the end of the string, record the partition.

questions.title: N-Queens
questions.statement: Place `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal). Return every distinct arrangement as a list of board strings using `'Q'` and `'.'`.
questions.approach: Place one queen per row, trying each column. Track used columns and both diagonals in boolean arrays (`row - col` and `row + col` identify diagonals) so each check is O(1). Backtrack when no column is free.

questions.title: Number of Islands
questions.statement: The grid contains `'1'` (land) and `'0'` (water). Return the number of islands, where an island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically.
questions.approach: Scan every cell. When you find unvisited land, count one island and flood-fill (DFS or BFS) all connected land, sinking it to `'0'` so it is not counted again. Each cell is visited at most twice.

questions.title: Clone Graph
questions.statement: Given a reference to a node of a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the whole graph. Each node has an integer value and a list of neighbours.

tests.output: a new graph with the same shape and values (no shared nodes)

questions.approach: DFS (or BFS) with a map from original node to its clone. If a node was already cloned, return the existing clone; this also breaks cycles. Otherwise create the clone, register it, then clone each neighbour.

questions.title: Max Area of Island
questions.statement: In a binary grid, an island is a group of `1`s connected horizontally or vertically. Return the area (number of cells) of the largest island, or 0 if there is none.
questions.approach: DFS from every land cell, returning 1 plus the areas of its four neighbours and sinking each visited cell to 0. Track the largest area returned.

questions.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
questions.target: O(M · N) Time (Reverse DFS from oceans)
questions.statement: `heights[r][c]` is the height of a cell. The Pacific Ocean touches the top and left edges, the Atlantic touches the bottom and right edges. Water flows to neighbouring cells of equal or lower height. Return all cells from which water can reach both oceans.
questions.approach: Run the search in reverse: start from the ocean borders and climb to neighbours that are equal or higher. Do this once for each ocean, then keep the cells reached by both.

questions.title: Surrounded Regions
questions.statement: A board contains `'X'` and `'O'`. Capture every region of `'O'` that is completely surrounded by `'X'` by flipping its cells to `'X'`. An `'O'` on the border, or connected to one, is not captured.
questions.approach: Work backwards from the border: mark every `'O'` reachable from a border `'O'` as safe (`'T'`). Then flip the remaining `'O'` to `'X'` and turn `'T'` back to `'O'`.

questions.title: Rotting Oranges
questions.statement: In a grid, `0` is empty, `1` is a fresh orange and `2` is a rotten orange. Every minute, each fresh orange next to a rotten one (up, down, left, right) becomes rotten. Return the minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if that is impossible.
questions.approach: Multi-source BFS: start with all rotten oranges in the queue and spread one level per minute, counting the fresh oranges that get infected. If any fresh orange is left at the end, return -1.

questions.title: Walls and Gates
questions.statement: A grid of rooms holds `-1` (wall), `0` (gate) and `2147483647` (empty room, "INF"). Fill each empty room with the number of steps to its nearest gate, or leave it as INF if no gate is reachable.
questions.approach: Multi-source BFS from every gate at once. The first time BFS reaches an empty room is by the shortest path, so assign `distance + 1` and enqueue it. Rooms never reached keep INF.

questions.title: Course Schedule
questions.target: O(V + E) Time (Topological Sort / Kahn's Algorithm / Cycle DFS)
questions.statement: There are `numCourses` courses labelled `0..n-1`. Each pair `[a, b]` means you must take course `b` before course `a`. Return whether all courses can be finished.
questions.approach: This is cycle detection in a directed graph. Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take courses with in-degree 0, "remove" them and reduce their dependents' in-degree. If every course gets taken, there is no cycle.

questions.title: Course Schedule II
questions.statement: Same setup as Course Schedule, but return one valid order in which to take all courses. If it is impossible, return an empty array.
questions.approach: Run Kahn's topological sort and record courses in the order they are taken. If fewer than `numCourses` were taken, a cycle exists and the answer is empty.

questions.title: Redundant Connection
questions.statement: A tree with `n` nodes had one extra edge added, creating a cycle. Given the edges, return the extra edge to remove so the graph becomes a tree again. If several answers exist, return the one that occurs last in the input.
questions.approach: Union-Find (disjoint set). Process edges in order; an edge whose endpoints already share a root would close a cycle, so it is the redundant one. Path compression plus union by size keeps each operation near O(1).

questions.title: Word Ladder
questions.statement: Transform `beginWord` into `endWord` by changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in `wordList`. Return the number of words in the shortest sequence (including both ends), or 0 if no sequence exists.
questions.approach: Shortest path in an implicit graph, so use BFS. From each word, try replacing every position with each letter `a-z` and keep results found in the dictionary that were not visited. The BFS level at which `endWord` appears is the answer.

questions.title: Climbing Stairs
questions.statement: You climb a staircase of `n` steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.
questions.approach: The ways to reach step `i` equal the ways to reach `i-1` plus the ways to reach `i-2` (the Fibonacci recurrence). Only the last two values are needed, so space is O(1).

questions.title: House Robber
questions.statement: Each house holds some money, and robbing two adjacent houses triggers an alarm. Return the maximum amount you can rob in one night.
questions.approach: At each house choose the better of skipping it (keep the previous best) or robbing it (value plus the best from two houses back). Two rolling variables are enough.

questions.title: House Robber II
questions.statement: The houses are arranged in a circle, so the first and last houses are adjacent. Return the maximum amount you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses.
questions.approach: Because the first and last houses cannot both be robbed, the answer is the better of two linear problems: houses `0..n-2` and houses `1..n-1`. Handle a single house separately.

questions.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
questions.target: O(N^2) Time, O(1) Space (Expand around center)
questions.statement: Return the longest palindromic substring of `s`.
questions.approach: Expand around every possible centre: each character (odd length) and each gap between characters (even length). Grow while both ends match and remember the longest span. O(N²) time, O(1) space.

questions.title: Decode Ways
questions.statement: Letters are encoded as `A=1 ... Z=26`. Given a digit string `s`, return the number of ways to decode it into letters.
questions.approach: `dp[i]` is the number of ways to decode the first `i` characters. A single digit adds `dp[i-1]` if it is 1-9; a two-digit number 10-26 adds `dp[i-2]`. Keep only the last two values.

questions.title: Coin Change
questions.statement: Given coin denominations and a target `amount`, return the fewest coins needed to make that amount, or -1 if it cannot be made. You have unlimited coins of each kind.
questions.approach: Bottom-up DP: `dp[a]` is the minimum coins for amount `a`. For each amount try every coin: `dp[a] = min(dp[a - coin] + 1)`. Initialise with a value larger than any answer to mark unreachable amounts.

questions.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
questions.target: O(N log N) Time (Patience Sorting + Binary Search)
questions.statement: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of `nums` (elements keep their order but need not be adjacent).
questions.approach: Patience sorting: keep `tails[k]`, the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length `k+1`. For each number, binary search the first tail that is at least it and replace that tail (or append). The size of `tails` is the answer.

questions.title: Word Break
questions.statement: Return whether string `s` can be split into a sequence of one or more words from the dictionary `wordDict`. Words may be reused.
